description: Cube clears can happen with more pieces. Possible to combo here.

A: Can be a combo. Clearing the line leaves the cube easier to clear.
B: No combo. Clearing the line make the cube hard to clear.
Gaps in corners are very hard to correct.

A: Clearing either line leave the other line easy to clear.
B: Clearing either line creates a gap in the other line.

A: Many pieces can clear the line.
B: Harder to clear the line near the edge.

A: Easy to clear via cube or line.
B: Take more cubes to clear.

A: The 2 bottom corners need different 3 square L shapes.
B: The 2 bottom corners need the same shape to clear.

A: Either diagonal shape can clear.
B: Only 1 diagonal shape can clear.

A: Cube clear is easy
B: Cube clear receives interference
B: Likely to cause problems if clearing a line.

The exception to prefer-middle: for the ring, the corner is better. It clears more at every horizon measured, and by 0.805 squares on the next set.

Mined from play, then stripped to the 5 squares the mistake needs (it started at 22). Two placements of one piece from one parent. A keeps a run of 3 unbroken where B leaves 2, and A's fullest line reaches 3 against 3. Nothing in the eval scores how near a line is to completing, so the broken version looks no worse. It prefers B by 4092; A clears 0.77 more squares on the next set.

Mined from play, then stripped to the 11 squares the mistake needs (it started at 21). Two placements of one piece from one parent. B puts 3 squares on the board edge against A's 1. The edge is not counted as a boundary, so a piece flush against the wall reads as tidier than the same piece extending a line inward — A's longest run is 6 against B's 3. The eval prefers B by 7565; A clears 0.99 more squares on the next set, counted over every hand.
